title: POC scoping: OpenAI-compat SDK + function calling integration — ArcadiaGov
summary: Initial POC scope for integrating Redwood Inference into ArcadiaGov's citizen services platform. Discussed success criteria (latency SLOs, throughput, cost per 1k tokens, and structured output reliability), workload sizing, benchmark plan, and integration choices: OpenAI-compatible endpoints vs native SDK, function/tool calling, and JSON schema enforcement. Security checklist and pilot timeline agreed: 6-8 week pilot with a 2-week benchmark sprint.
topics: Benchmarks: p50/p95/p99 targets and load profiles
Integration options: SDKs vs OpenAI-compat endpoints
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (ArcadiaGov CTO), Liam O'Connor (Platform Lead), Rosa Martinez (Security Eng), Samir Patel (Dev Lead)

Summary (auto):
- ArcadiaGov wants a POC to replace heuristic rules in their citizen request triage with an LLM-backed assistant. Primary constraints are latency (for UI response), auditability (structured output + audit logs), and on-prem/VPC acceptable deployment.
- Agreed initial success criteria: median latency < 220ms for short prompts (<= 400 tokens), p95 < 700ms, throughput ~150 req/s for the synchronous UI path; cost target ~<$0.003 per 1k tokens equivalent.
- Technical priorities: OpenAI-compatible endpoints for quick integration, but evaluate Redwood SDK for advanced batching and KV cache benefits. Function calling required for lookup actions (citizen profile, case creation).
- Security asks: SOC2 + SSO/SAML, KMS integration for key management, audit log retention 2 years.
- Pilot timeline: 6 week pilot (2 weeks bench sprint, 3 weeks integration, 1 week validation), handshake on next steps: share benchmark template, security pack, and schedule kickoff for Dec 4.

-- Transcript body (timestamps are approximate, transcription may contain errors):
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Diego our solutions engineer. How're you all doing?
[00:04] Priya Nair: Good, thanks. Busy, but excited to see how this could simplify our triage flow.
[00:09] Liam O'Connor: Hi, yeah we got a packed calendar but we sketched out some requirements ahead of time.
[00:15] Diego Alvarez: Awesome. On the agenda — scope the POC, define success criteria, talk workloads and bench plan, and integration path — OpenAI-compat versus Redwood SDK.
[00:25] Samir Patel: Quick note — our UI requires sub-second responses for the agent path, otherwise user frustration is high. We consider anything above ~700ms as a failure for primary flows.
[00:33] Rosa Martinez: And for us security: we need auditability and encrypted keys, plus the ability to host inside our VPC. SOC2 is baseline.
[00:42] Maya Chen: Understood — we typically recommend an initial benchmark that mirrors your UI flow: short prompts (200–400 tokens), and a fallback batch/async path for longer generative tasks. Diego, wanna run the latency numbers we usually target?
[00:52] Diego Alvarez: Sure — on our hosted infra with optimized kernels we see p50 ~120–180ms for short prompts on gpus with continuous batching disabled for interactive routes; p95 tends to be around 400–600ms depending on concurrency. With Redwood Dedicated and tuned batching you can push throughput higher and reduce cost, but dedicated adds procurement.
[01:15] Priya Nair: Could you clarify "continuous batching disabled" — we need predictable latencies not 2 second wait for a batch to fill.
[01:22] Diego Alvarez: Right, for interactive SLOs you'd set max batching latency very low or route to a low-latency profile; continuous batching is optional and better for background workloads.
[01:30] Liam O'Connor: For sizing — our peak concurrent interactive sessions are around 120 users, avg 1 req per 6s, but we also get spikes up to 300 concurrent during policy events. Token sizes: average 250 tokens request, response 150 tokens.
[01:44] Maya Chen: Good, that's concrete. For the POC we'll simulate both normal and spike patterns. We'll want you to confirm tokenization behavior — some internal abbreviations trip token counts.
[01:53] Samir Patel: Right, we'll provide sample prompts and a small dump of typical messages — sanitized.
[01:58] Rosa Martinez: On the audit front, we need immutable logs and structured outputs — e.g., JSON schema with fields: action, confidence, case_id (nullable), and redactions.
[02:09] Diego Alvarez: We support structured JSON outputs and schema validation hooks; function calling can make the assistant return strongly typed payloads. Our OpenAI-compatible endpoints also support the function calling format so minimal code change.
[02:20] Priya Nair: Is there any mismatch between Redwood's function calling and OpenAI's? We use an internal lightweight adapter today.
[02:27] Diego Alvarez: Generally it's compatible; there are a few variant field names in older SDKs. For the POC recommended path: start with OpenAI-compat endpoints to validate product fit quickly, then move to Redwood SDK if you want advanced batching, KV cache, and lower unit costs.
[02:41] Liam O'Connor: What about structured output reliability? We need >95% exact schema conformance on the primary fields.
[02:48] Maya Chen: That's reasonable. We'll run schema-conformance tests during the bench sprint. If model outputs drift, we can enforce deterministic function calling or apply post-processing validators.
[02:57] Samir Patel: For function calling, we need the assistant to call an internal microservice to fetch citizen records — that service is behind our VPC. How do you handle connectivity for private deployments?
[03:07] Diego Alvarez: For Redwood Private you'll host inference in your VPC with a customer-managed control plane, so function calls can be proxied to internal endpoints. For hosted, we'd recommend a secure webhook with mTLS and IP allowlist, but that adds network setup.
[03:20] Rosa Martinez: Security question — KMS/HSM and key rotation policies?
[03:24] Maya Chen: Supported. Redwood Private supports KMS integration (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, and HSM-based providers). We can share our security pack with the exact controls and SOC2 cert.
[03:33] Priya Nair: Great. On benchmarks — what's a typical bench plan you run for a POC?
[03:38] Diego Alvarez: We propose a 10-day benchmark sprint: 2 days onboarding and sample collection, 5 days of load testing (baseline + 2 spike days), and 3 days of analysis and tuning. We capture p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec throughput, failure rates, and cost modelling. We'll provide a spreadsheet template.
[03:54] Liam O'Connor: That timeline maps well to our internal windows — we were hoping to run bench the week after next.
[03:59] Maya Chen: We can start Dec 8 for bench if we kickoff Dec 4; that gives time to exchange test data and security checks.
[04:06] Samir Patel: Integration work — we prefer OpenAI-compat endpoints first. How much code change to switch to Redwood SDK later?
[04:12] Diego Alvarez: Minimal for simple calls — endpoints accept the same payloads. If you adopt Redwood SDK later to leverage KV cache and batching you'd add a small client library and change the call surface for streaming/advanced options. We'll provide migration notes.
[04:25] Priya Nair: Do you support streaming JSON chunks? We want to render a partial structured response as it arrives in the UI.
[04:31] Diego Alvarez: Yes, streaming with partial JSON is supported. We recommend using a guardrail schema and an incremental parser on the client to avoid broken states.
[04:40] Rosa Martinez: About logging — can we get token-level cost breakdowns per request for auditing?
[04:45] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, latency per route, and per-token KPIs. We can also export logs to your SIEM for retention.
[04:53] Priya Nair: Competitors: we looked briefly at running with OpenAI directly, and also Alpaca/Anthropic self-host options, mainly to compare cost and data residency. Is Redwood offering any absolute cost sheet?
[05:04] Maya Chen: We'll share a modeled cost sheet—benchmarks will prove unit economics. For upfront guidance, expect hosted to be easiest; dedicated provides predictable rates and is better if you want reserved throughput.
[05:14] Liam O'Connor: Ok, next steps — what do you need from us?
[05:18] Maya Chen: We'll need: sanitized sample prompts and user sessions, an IP for sending test webhooks (or details for VPC peering), security questionnaire responses, and a list of stakeholders for the POC.
[05:28] Samir Patel: We'll anonymize data and send a tokenized subset by Monday.
[05:32] Priya Nair: Security will fill in the questionnaire — Rosa will own that.
[05:36] Rosa Martinez: Yep I'll fill it and try to get back by Nov 30.
[05:40] Diego Alvarez: I'll email the benchmark template and a Redweood (sic) quickstart link for OpenAI-compat endpoints.
[05:45] Maya Chen: Great — to recap we'll schedule the POC kickoff on Dec 4; bench sprint starts Dec 8. Success criteria recap: p50 <220ms, p95 <700ms for interactive route, schema conformance >95%, throughput target 150 req/s baseline, and acceptable cost metric.
[05:59] Priya Nair: That sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[06:02] Liam O'Connor: Thanks, talk soon.
